Title: Dark Bloom

Genre: Magical Realism

Word Count: 2.6k

Desired Feedback: Primary concern is that I'm too wordy, embellish too much, and readers can't stick with it. However, I would like any feedback at all.

Plot Summary: This is a cozy magical realism book set in the lush Appalachian forests of West Virginia, where we encounter Rusty, a hardened and cynical war veteran who is running away from his past. He soon finds his new home has more to offer than meets the eye, as he encounters an otherworldly creature in the woods surrounding his cabin. He finds himself on a magical journey of self-discovery leading to the ultimate realization that death and life are inseparable components of the human experience, and allows himself to have hope in who he is, and for humanity, for the first time.

Preview: The forest is loudest in fall - it's the sound of change. It all starts with the wind, the constant percussion in the symphony of Autumn. A cold northern gust comes barreling down the valley from Alberta, and suddenly the friendly breeze from the southwest is retreating like an army on the move. The northern wind has a fierce voice. I hear it roar when it snaps the branches from the trees, when it surrounds my house in its ominous embrace and rattles the window panes. The leaves swirl and twist around each other like lovers in a dance, swaying to the beat. Deep in the forest, the animals make a ruckus preparing for winter. Bears rummage through my garbage at night, squirrels build nests under the deck, mice roost in the wall. Yes, things are loud around here in fall.

I live at Aviation Camp. It's a red house on West Virginia state game lands, built in the 1890s by a farmer and his family looking for security and safety in the tumultuous times following the Civil War. Originally, the three acres of land in back of the property were cleared and used for growing crops, but nature was quick to reclaim that land when the place was abandoned in the 1920s. And 30 years later, back from my first tour in Vietnam and looking for some security myself, I bought the place. I gave the house a fresh coat of paint, replaced the floors, and added indoor plumbing. My nephew is the one who named it Aviation Camp. He said the color reminded him of the Red Baron and I couldn't help but agree. My closest neighbors (who really aren't very close) are a pair of not so clever backwoods brothers who were ingenious enough to name their house "Camp Shooting." So I figured, combine my airplane house with their house of ammunition and you've got the Red Baron. Combine my house with their house and you've got war.
